learningObjectives: Distinguish alerting, orienting and executive aspects of attention.
Compare dorsal and ventral attention systems.
Explain reorienting without reducing attention to one spotlight.
Use mechanism-focused language when formulating inattention.

anatomy.label: Dorsal attention network
anatomy.detail: Intraparietal and frontal eye-field regions bias sensory processing toward current goals.
anatomy.clinical: Weak top-down selection may look like distractibility or poor task persistence.

anatomy.label: Ventral attention network
anatomy.detail: Right-lateralised temporoparietal and ventral frontal regions respond to unexpected, relevant events.
anatomy.clinical: Disruption can contribute to spatial neglect and impaired reorienting.

anatomy.label: Alerting systems
anatomy.detail: Brainstem, thalamic and cortical systems regulate tonic and phasic readiness.
anatomy.clinical: Low arousal and poor sleep can mimic or worsen attentional disorder.

anatomy.label: Orienting systems
anatomy.detail: Orienting can be overt through eye movements or covert without moving the eyes.
anatomy.clinical: Biases may be spatial, sensory or conceptual.

anatomy.label: Executive attention
anatomy.detail: Control systems help sustain a goal when distractors or competing responses are strong.
anatomy.clinical: Anxiety, reward and working-memory load can alter this function.

interaction.title: Attention Networks sequence
interaction.instruction: Select a component, then run the sequence to follow information flow across the network.

stages.label: Alert
stages.text: Establish sufficient readiness to process information.

stages.label: Select
stages.text: Bias processing toward the current goal.

stages.label: Interrupt
stages.text: Detect a relevant event outside the current focus.

stages.label: Reorient
stages.text: Shift attention and update the active priority.

quizBank.question: The dorsal attention network primarily supports:
quizBank.explanation: The dorsal system supports top-down orienting and selection.

quizBank.question: The ventral attention network is especially involved in:
quizBank.explanation: It helps interrupt and redirect attention.

quizBank.question: Alerting differs from orienting because alerting concerns:
options: Readiness, whereas orienting selects a target
Vision only, whereas orienting controls hearing
Movement only, whereas orienting controls sleep
quizBank.explanation: Alerting establishes readiness; orienting allocates selection.

quizBank.question: Spatial neglect is best understood as:
options: A distributed attention-network disorder, often after right hemisphere injury
A memory disorder with no attentional component
quizBank.explanation: Neglect reflects disrupted attention networks rather than simple blindness.

quizBank.question: Clinically, “inattention” should prompt questions about:
options: Arousal, selection, disengagement, reward and overload
quizBank.explanation: Several mechanisms can produce the same behavioural label.
